flawed_step: Step 1 holds: if G is isomorphic to its complement, the two have the same number of edges, so 2|E(G)| = C(n,2). Step 2 fails: a construction for every n >= 4 would need C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 to be even for every n >= 4. That is true only when n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). It fails for n = 6 (and 7, 10, 11, ...).
counterexample: n = 6: C(6,2) = 15 is odd. A self-complementary graph would need 15/2 edges, which is impossible, so no self-complementary graph on 6 vertices exists.
assessment_summary: An isomorphism keeps the number of edges the same. So if G is self-complementary, G and its complement each have half of all C(n,2) possible edges, and n(n-1)/4 must be a whole number. That forces n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). For n = 6 there are 15 possible edges, an odd number, so no self-complementary graph on 6 vertices exists. The proof attempt stops at the step that would need C(n,2) to be even for all n >= 4. The statement is false.
